buildSteps.title: Pick and prepare the site
buildSteps.detail: Choose a spot near ice or useful minerals but clear of unstable ground. Robots level a pad and pile up berms for blast and radiation shielding.

buildSteps.title: Mine and grade the regolith
buildSteps.detail: Surface material is dug, crushed and sieved to a consistent grain size, then dried to drive off volatiles that would spoil the mix.

buildSteps.title: Mix the feedstock
buildSteps.detail: The regolith is blended either with a binder that sets chemically, or left dry for thermal sintering, in a hopper feeding the print head.

buildSteps.title: Print a calibration article
buildSteps.detail: A small test wall is printed and its strength and porosity measured, so the machine can correct its own settings before the real build.

buildSteps.title: Print the shell
buildSteps.detail: The head traces the dome or vault layer by layer, a few millimetres to centimetres at a time, with a steep angle so the fresh layers support themselves.

buildSteps.title: Cure or sinter
buildSteps.detail: Each pass is fused by laser, microwave or concentrated sunlight at over 1000 °C, or left to cure if a binder is used, until the shell is solid rock-like mass.

buildSteps.title: Install the pressure envelope
buildSteps.detail: An inflatable or metallic core is placed inside or printed around, connected to the airlock, and the interior is fitted out with floors and life support.

buildSteps.title: Pressurise and commission
buildSteps.detail: The module is filled with air, leak-tested, powered up and monitored; only then is it safe for crew.

prerequisites.why: with no builders on site, the printer must excavate, print and self-correct without help.
microwave, laser and solar sintering plus geopolymer and sulphur binders have been proven only on Earth with simulants.
no mission has yet mined, processed and built with extraterrestrial material; every gram so far has been launched.
printing and sintering draw continuous kilowatts through the lunar night or Martian dust storms.

prerequisites.tech: Airtight habitat modules and life support
prerequisites.why: pressurised inflatables have been tested in orbit, but not combined with a printed outer shell.
several metres of regolith are needed to replace Earth's atmosphere, and that mass has to be printed, not carried.

pathway.milestone: Earth-based demonstrations printing with regolith simulant, following NASA's 3D-Printed Habitat Challenge that ran from 2015 to 2019
pathway.unlocks: proven extrusion and sintering methods, plus material strength data.

pathway.milestone: uncrewed lunar landers carrying small printers to build landing pads, berms and shielding walls
pathway.unlocks: the first structures made off Earth, on a low-risk non-pressurised target.

pathway.milestone: a robotically printed and pressurised demonstration module on the Moon
pathway.unlocks: confidence that printed shells can hold air and shelter crews, and a repeatable construction recipe.

pathway.milestone: crewed habitats printed on Mars from local regolith
pathway.unlocks: settlements that grow without shipping every wall from Earth; in-orbit printing of large structures from recycled material is a parallel track.
